demand_source.title: Delegate architecture
demand_source.supports: OpenClaw describes read-only calendar access (read events, surface conflicts, summarize the day) as the lowest-risk tier of what an assistant agent does for the people it serves.

edits.example: Jordan texts: 'What's on Saturday?' and gets the day's events from the family calendar. Tony asks 'is anyone free Friday at 1?' and gets what the family calendar shows for that hour and whose event it is; nothing on the calendar is changed.
caveats: Public feeds (the school district calendar, library and recreation events, team schedules) show up in Happy's calendar answers only after the family Google Calendar is subscribed to each feed link, which Google allows from a computer browser only; a search of the installed OpenClaw docs and skills found no .ics handling of its own. Google gives no refresh interval and TeamSnap says changes can take up to 24 hours to appear, so change alerts are a separate job (the model-free watchers, F018).

'Is anyone free?' is answered only from events the asking parent's sign-in can see: the family calendar, and that parent's own calendars unless the tool can be pinned to one calendar. The other parent's work or personal calendar is not read, so 'free' means 'nothing on the family calendar'. gog's server offers one calendar tool, the events list, and no free/busy tool; reading each parent's own calendar as busy-only is the wider grant described under the conflict watch (MKT-06).
edits.safety: Read-only and calendar-only by construction: each account is added for the Calendar service alone with gog's --readonly switch, which asks Google for read-only access and blocks changes at runtime, and the server is narrowed to the events-listing tool. Without those two limits the sign-in would cover gog's default set of Google services rather than Calendar alone, and the server would register every read tool it has, mail and Drive search among them, on the agent that holds a parent's memory, which the roadmap keeps apart from mail. Event titles and descriptions can be written by people outside the family (an invitation, a subscribed public feed), and OpenClaw says its sender controls do not sanitize tool results (hardened-baseline.md:42), so calendar text is outside content read by that agent. It cannot browse and its texts are pinned to the family (G009); the one way out that is neither closed nor pinned is the hand-off to the research helper (F019), which the roadmap names as the remaining leak path.

reason: Kept: reading a public page is a built-in OpenClaw tool, and eight entries build on this helper. One detail behind the promise that the helper cannot reach the home network was not recorded. The block depends on the fetch tool checking the resolved address itself, and the documented switch that sends fetches through an operator's proxy (the roadmap plans such a proxy) hands that check to the proxy. The entry now says to leave that switch off unless the proxy refuses private addresses, and adds a matching test case.

demand_source.title: Web fetch
demand_source.supports: OpenClaw's built-in page fetcher gets a URL and returns its readable text, which is what lets the helper answer from a public page.

caveats: The plain fetch runs no JavaScript and cannot log in, so such pages wait for the research browser (F020) or stay unread.

web_fetch blocks private hosts and re-checks redirects, but the browser's own check is weaker (the docs say its request interception is not a network firewall), which matters once F020 switches the browser on.

Leave the private-network keys truly unset: an explicitly written `browser.ssrfPolicy.dangerouslyAllowPrivateNetwork: false` turns hostname navigation into an allowlist and would stop a later research browser from loading hostnames.

The SSRF policy covers the `web_fetch` and browser tools only, so host-side helpers that take a URL (the summarize wrapper, the print plugin's download, watcher scripts) need their own scheme, host and resolved-address checks.

A hostname block list is not an exfiltration control and is not worth curating: what counts is the private-network block, no headers, no fallback provider, and no private data in the agent that browses.

Once research has web_fetch, the roadmap's egress proxy cannot double as an exfiltration allowlist; it can deny private ranges and named hosts and nothing more (an inference from the routing description).
A sandboxed requester cannot spawn an unsandboxed target, so research has to stay sandboxed, and sub-agents keep only AGENTS.md, so every citation and no-login rule must be in that one file.
An official-sites-only mode for admin questions would need a before_tool_call hook and is not planned.

The home-network block rests on the fetch tool resolving and pinning the address itself. If web_fetch is ever routed through the roadmap's egress proxy with `tools.web.fetch.useTrustedEnvProxy: true`, OpenClaw keeps only the hostname check and leaves address resolution to the proxy, so that switch stays off unless the proxy denies private ranges after it resolves the name.
